title: Russian Matryoshka Doll
facts: This is a matryoshka, a set of Russian wooden nesting dolls that stack inside one another, from one large doll down to a tiny solid doll at the center.
The name matryoshka comes from Matryona, a very common Russian peasant name at the time, which was chosen because it evoked a warm, fertile mother figure with many children nested inside her.
The first matryoshka set was carved in 1890 by craftsman Vasily Zvyozdochkin and painted by artist Sergey Malyutin, working at the Children's Education workshop near Moscow.
The idea was inspired by a Japanese nesting figure of the seven lucky gods that had been brought back to Russia, which the Russian artists reimagined as a peasant family instead.

A classic matryoshka is painted as a young woman in a traditional sarafan dress and a headscarf, holding something like a basket, a rooster, or flowers, with smaller versions of herself nested inside.
Because each smaller doll is literally contained within the larger one, matryoshkas became a popular symbol of motherhood, family, and generations of a family holding each other together.
The dolls are turned on a lathe from well-dried linden or birch wood, hollowed out from the inside so that each piece fits snugly inside the next size up.
Matryoshkas won a bronze medal at the 1900 World's Fair in Paris, and that international attention is a big part of why they became famous outside Russia as a national symbol.

While the traditional design is a peasant woman, modern matryoshka sets are made depicting almost anything, from folk tale characters to world leaders, and sets can range from just a few dolls to fifty or more nested pieces.

In a matryoshka set, the largest outer doll conventionally represents a mother figure, and each smaller doll nested inside represents one of her children, which is why the toy is so strongly tied to themes of family.
Sets traditionally come in odd numbers of dolls, often three, five, or seven, though larger collector's sets can include a dozen or more nested pieces.
Before carving begins, the linden or birch wood is seasoned for one to two years so it won't crack or warp once turned and hollowed on the lathe.
After the wood pieces are shaped and dried, artisans hand-paint each doll and then usually finish it with a clear lacquer coat, which both protects the paint and gives the doll its glossy shine.
The town of Sergiev Posad, near Moscow, became one of Russia's most famous centers of matryoshka production and is sometimes nicknamed the toy capital of Russia.
Semyonov and Polkhovsky Maidan are two other Russian towns especially well known for their own distinct regional matryoshka painting styles, each with recognizable color patterns and floral motifs.

Specialty matryoshka sets have been painted to depict entire fairy tales, the line of Russian tsars, or caricatures of world leaders, especially popular as novelty gifts and political satire since the late twentieth century.
The largest matryoshka sets made by specialty artisans have included over fifty nested dolls, created as showpieces for exhibitions and serious collectors rather than everyday souvenirs.
Matryoshka dolls are commonly sold at Russian tourist markets such as Moscow's Izmaylovo Market, and have become one of the most internationally recognized symbols of Russian folk craft.

Because the smallest doll in a set is solid wood with no cavity, losing or swapping it means the whole nested set can no longer close completely, which is why complete original sets are especially valued by collectors.
